title: Roundup #88: Is it time to panic yet?
gist: Weekly roundup: bipartisan public support for slowing AI is surging against a Trump/investor/libertarian/hawk/progressive-skeptic coalition; economists doubt AI-driven 15% growth; SaaS revenue and stocks recovered after the early-2026 'SaaSpocalypse'; plus pass-through 'everywhere millionaires', NYC MTA state-capacity wins, and Glaeser's case that self-driving cars favor dense cities.

insights.claim: Five groups oppose an AI slowdown: the Trump administration (fearing slower growth), investors worried about returns, libertarians and techno-optimists, China hawks, and progressives who have argued AI doesn't work or is a bubble.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Maps the political coalition protecting AI capex; its erosion would raise regulatory risk for AI names.
insights.locator: There are five main groups of people opposing

insights.claim: Polling compiled by Nate Silver shows a bipartisan majority worried about existential AI risk and a bipartisan majority saying AI is moving too fast.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Broad public support for slowing AI raises the odds of regulation affecting AI labs and hyperscaler capex.
insights.locator: A bipartisan majority is now worried

insights.claim: Progressives are split in a civil war between 'AI is dangerous' (Bernie Sanders) and 'AI is fake' (David Sirota) camps, while Barack Obama urges Democrats to make AI safety a tentpole issue.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI safety may become a core Democratic campaign plank, shaping post-election tech policy.
insights.locator: In fact, in recent days there has

insights.claim: Trump is resisting the tide of public opinion on AI slowdown, as he has on the Iran War and tariffs, but Smith doubts he can hold out for long.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A White House shift toward AI restraint is a live risk for AI-exposed equities.
insights.locator: This is remarkable. I don't think

insights.claim: A public bet organized by Ben Moll on whether AI delivers explosive growth has a $425,000 pot, with AI researchers mostly on the fast-growth side and economists mostly on the slow side, including a split within Google DeepMind.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A visible gauge of the gap between AI-industry and economist growth expectations.
insights.locator: There's a pretty epic public bet

insights.claim: Fast-growth bettors forecast 15% annual growth, far above the 5.3% that AI experts gave as their most optimistic scenario in Forecasting Research Institute data; China hit 15% only once (1984) since its rapid growth began.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Macro assumptions baked into AI valuations may be far more aggressive than expert consensus.
insights.locator: But the people publicly betting on fast growth

insights.claim: Imas and Moll list brakes on near-term AI growth: slow diffusion, a productivity J-curve, difficulty automating the physical world, political barriers, reorganizing production, a persistent human 'relational sector', bottlenecked inputs like chips, Baumol's cost disease, and AI disasters slowing adoption.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Checklist for tracking whether AI productivity gains show up in GDP; chip bottlenecks favor supply-constrained semis.
insights.locator: Basically, they foresee a bunch of factors

insights.claim: Smith leans toward the economists' measured growth expectations but is open to upside surprise.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests skepticism toward macro narratives priced for double-digit AI-driven growth.

insights.claim: In early 2026 enterprise software stocks lost nearly $1 trillion in value by early February, perhaps $2 trillion including subsequent weeks, on fears coding agents would replace SaaS.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shows how fast narrative-driven AI-disruption selloffs can hit software valuations.
insights.locator: The SaaSpocalypse was more like a RenaiSaaS

insights.claim: Stripe Economics (Ernie Tedeschi) found an index of public SaaS companies grew revenue faster after coding agents launched, and SaaS stocks have recovered all the ground they lost.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI-disruption selloffs in incumbents can be buying opportunities when revenue data doesn't confirm the narrative.
insights.locator: Earlier this year, when coding agents came out

insights.claim: Smith argues AI is acting as a complement rather than a substitute across the economy: companies still buy software rather than build it with coding agents, and SaaS firms raise their own productivity with AI, echoing AI's failure so far to kill jobs or Indian back-office outsourcing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of 'AI kills sector X' trades; watch for new AI-native business models as the real disruption risk.
insights.quote: AI is proving to be a complement when people thought it was going to be a substitute.

insights.claim: Zidar and Zwick estimate about 1.7 million Americans have built at least $10 million in net worth by owning a private business, and for every public-company CEO there are over 1,000 private-business owners worth more than $25 million.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: US top wealth is concentrated in private pass-through businesses, a large target market for wealth management and private-markets products.

insights.claim: Pass-through business owners benefit from tax loopholes, such as avoiding Medicare taxes and estate-tax exemptions letting a married couple pass $30 million tax-free, so business income is taxed much less than wages.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Pass-through tax treatment is a potential target in future tax reform; relevant for private-business valuations and succession planning.

insights.claim: Erick Erickson exposed a network around Charles Haywood whose foundation gave the Claremont Institute $390,500 since 2022, with ties to the Society for American Civic Renewal and figures at New Founding and the Blaze, distinct from Nick Fuentes's groyper network; both reportedly have ties to JD Vance.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: An intra-Right conflict between Christian conservatives and extremist factions could shape the post-Trump GOP and its policy direction.

insights.claim: NYC's MTA finished the Park Avenue Viaduct project 60 months ahead of schedule and $195 million under a $960 million budget after consolidating capital work into MTA Construction & Development in 2019, using design-build contracts, bundled procurement and more in-house work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shows US infrastructure cost overruns are fixable with institutional reform; relevant to infrastructure contractors and muni project risk.

insights.claim: MTA C&D awarded over $8 billion in contracts in 2023 at prices 6.2% below engineer estimates, saving nearly $300 million, and reported another $1.2 billion in savings in 2025, while L.A.'s D Line extension remains mired in delays and overruns.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Execution quality varies widely across US transit agencies; the political will for state capacity is the key variable.

insights.claim: Ed Glaeser argues self-driving cars will modestly increase demand for dense urban living, because urbanites spend more time commuting than suburbanites and benefit more from autonomous trips.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Contradicts the sprawl thesis for autonomous vehicles; supportive of urban real estate rather than exurban land plays.
